answer:
**Pearson correlation measures linear association; mutual information measures general statistical dependence.** Zero correlation does not imply independence except under special distributional assumptions, such as joint Gaussianity. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)[2](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book2.html)

Take a discrete variable $X$ uniformly distributed over $\{-1,0,1\}$ and set $Y=X^2$. Then $E[X]=0$, and $E[XY]=E[X^3]=0$. Both variables have positive variance, so their Pearson correlation is zero. Yet observing $Y=0$ tells you exactly that $X=0$, and observing $Y=1$ rules that value out. They are clearly dependent.

For discrete variables,

$$I(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}=H(Y)-H(Y\mid X).$$

Here $Y$ is determined by $X$, so $H(Y\mid X)=0$. Since $P(Y=0)=1/3$ and $P(Y=1)=2/3$, the information is $-\frac13\log_2\frac13-\frac23\log_2\frac23\approx0.918$ bits. It is positive despite zero linear correlation.

Mutual information is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when the variables are independent, under the usual well-defined distributional setting. Unlike correlation, it has no positive/negative direction: it tells you that knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other, not whether one increases with the other.

**Estimation is the practical difficulty.** Sample correlation is simple to compute; mutual-information estimation for continuous or high-dimensional variables needs choices such as binning, density estimation, or nearest-neighbor methods. These choices introduce bias and sensitivity to sample size. A noisy MI estimate is not automatically a better feature-selection tool than a simple correlation screen. [3](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html)[5](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Finally, dependence is not causation. Both variables might reflect a common cause, and selecting features by association before splitting data can leak evaluation information. Fit any data-dependent selection procedure inside the training folds and validate its effect on the actual prediction task.
